L66: # Contingency Planning Guide for Federal Information Systems
L67: 
L68: Date Published: May 2010 (Updated 11/11/2010)
L69: 
L70: Supersedes: 【37†SP 800-34 Rev. 1 (05/31/2010)】

L74: #### Author(s)
L75: 
L76: Marianne Swanson (NIST), Pauline Bowen (NIST), Amy Phillips (BAH), Dean Gallup (BAH), David Lynes (BAH)
L77: #### Abstract
L78: This publication assists organizations in understanding the purpose, process, and format of information system contingency planning development through practical, real-world guidelines. This guidance document provides background information on interrelationships between information system contingency planning and other types of security and emergency management-related contingency plans, organizational resiliency, and the system development life cycle.
L79: This document provides guidance to help personnel evaluate information systems and operations to determine contingency planning requirements and priorities.

L64: ### NIST SP 800-184
L65: 
L66: # Guide for Cybersecurity Event Recovery
L67: 
L68: Date Published: December 2016
L69: 
L70: #### Author(s)
L71: 
L72: Michael Bartock (NIST), Jeffrey Cichonski (NIST), Murugiah Souppaya (NIST), Matthew Smith (G2), Gregory Witte (G2), Karen Scarfone (Scarfone Cybersecurity)
L73: #### Abstract
L74: In light of an increasing number of cybersecurity events, organizations can improve resilience by ensuring that their risk management processes include comprehensive recovery planning. Identifying and prioritizing organization resources helps to guide effective plans and realistic test scenarios. This preparation enables rapid recovery from incidents when they occur and helps to minimize the impact on the organization and its constituents.
L75: Additionally, continually improving recovery planning by learning lessons from past events, including those of other organizations, helps to ensure the continuity of important mission functions. This publication provides tactical and strategic guidance regarding the planning, playbook developing, testing, and improvement of recovery planning. It also provides an example scenario that demonstrates guidance and informative metrics that may be helpful for improving resilience of information systems.

L20: # Quality Training Standards
L21: 
L22: For Public Health
L23: 
L24: Oct. 1, 2026
L25: ## What to know
L26: 
L27:   * CDC's eight training standards serve as a quality benchmark for trainings developed or funded by CDC.
L28:   * A training must meet all eight standards to be considered a CDC Quality Training.
L29:   * The standards provide guidance for developing quality training that results in learning.
L30:   * These standards are for training developers to use in their training development process.
L31: 
L32: ## 1. Needs Assessment
L33: ### Training needs assessment informs training development.
L34:   * Ensure that training is needed to address the gap, 【3†training is not always the solution】.
L35:   * Conduct a 【4†needs assessment】 that validates the need for training.
L36:   * Consider a simple or complex approach.
L37:     * Complex approaches might include collecting new data through surveys and interviews.
L38:     * Simple approaches might include looking at existing data or literature or talking to a few key informants.
L39:   * Conduct a training needs analysis if training is needed. This is a part of the needs assessment and focuses on gathering information that helps with training approach.
L40:     * Identify and confirm the training goal with key partners.
L41:     * Identify and describe learners (and community if appropriate).
L42:     * Identify barriers and facilitators for training delivery (e.g., language, technology, or location).
L43:   * Select a delivery method(s), strategy(ies), or trainers appropriate for content and learners.
L44: Some trainings may require additional attributes. Consider if the following apply to your training:
L45: 
L46:   * Identify appropriate competencies (e.g., 【5†Core Competencies for Public Health Professionals】), if relevant.
L47:   * Establish and confer with a planning committee that includes representatives of the learner audience.
L48: ## 2. Learning Objectives
L49: ### Training includes learning objectives.
L50: 
L51:   * Develop SMART (Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, and Time-bound) learning objectives (e.g., 【6†writing effective learning objectives】).
L52:   * Match learning objectives with goals.
L53:   * Select educational methods that support learning objectives.
L54: 
L55: Some trainings may require additional attributes. Consider if the following apply to your training:
L56:   * Match learning objectives with competencies (e.g., 【5†Core Competencies for Public Health Professionals】), if competencies exist.
L57:   * Describe prerequisite knowledge and skills and how they can be obtained.
L58: ## 3. Accurate and Relevant
L59: ### Training content is accurate and relevant.
L60:   * Develop content that meets the needs of the learners and program based on the needs assessment.
L61:   * Consider your learners and make sure your content (including examples and visuals) is appropriate and relevant.
L62:     * Include real-world examples that support the content.
L63:   * Ensure content aligns with learning objectives to avoid unnecessary material.
L64:   * Conduct a 【7†subject matter expert (SME)†www.jsu.edu】 review.
L65:     * The SME(s) should ensure that content is accurate based on best-available evidence and up-to-date.
L66:     * The SME(s) should review for bias and ensure possible biases (including commercial bias) are minimized and mitigated (e.g., content changed and conflicts of interest disclosed).
L67:   * Create an expiration date for the training to review and update or retire, as needed.
L68:     * Review may include evidence-based practice, peer review journals, best practices, or SMEs' input.
L69:     * Update or remove content in a timely manner.
L70: Some trainings may require additional attributes. Consider if the following apply to your training:
L71:   * Align content with at least one professional competency (e.g., 【5†Core Competencies for Public Health Professionals】), if competencies exist.
L72:   * Ensure content offered in another language is 【8†linguistically appropriate and accurate†thinkculturalhealth.hhs.gov】. If it was translated and not created directly in the target language, verify that it was done using 【9†standard industry translation processes†www.astm.org】 and is reviewed by a bilingual SME(s).
L73: ## 4. Learner Engagement
L74: ### Training includes opportunities for learner engagement.
L75: 
L76:   * Design training that is interactive or engaging (e.g., knowledge checks, case studies, question and answer sessions, or exercises), as appropriate for learners' needs and training goals.
L77:   * Provide opportunity for learners to receive feedback.
L78:   * Facilitate engagement activities to include all learners.
L79: 
L80: Some trainings may require additional attributes. Consider if the following apply to your training:
L81:   * Use 【10†adult learning principles】 for adult learners.
L82:   * Include experiential or practice-based learning (e.g., internship with a mentor for on-the-job learning).
L83:   * Provide opportunity for learners to share experiences and learn from others' experiences. These may include peer learning and interdisciplinary opportunities for practice.
L84: ## 5. Usability and Accessibility
L85: ### Training is designed for usability and accessibility.
L86:   * Use conversational style that is appropriate for learners (i.e., active voice, present tense, and second person).
L87:   * Use language and tone that is 【11†familiar and clear for learners】.
L88:   * Select media, interface, and educational methods that can be used by your audience and facilitates learning (e.g., some learners may not have reliable internet access).
L89:   * Design for user experience.
L90:     * Develop easy and user-friendly navigation or materials.
L91:     * Ensure that navigation or materials allow learners flexibility to access content that that they need.
L92:     * Organize concepts in logical sections.
L93:   * Make content accessible to learners (e.g., 【12†section 508†www.section508.gov】 compliant and accommodations as needed).
L94: Some trainings may require additional attributes. Consider if the following apply to your training:
L95: 
L96:   * Use high quality (e.g., clear, clean, and crisp) audio and visual aids to clarify concepts when appropriate.
L97:   * Use technology that is current and easy to access.
L98:     * Ensure that links are functional.
L99:     * Provide technical support.
L100: ## 6. Evaluation
L101: ### Training evaluation informs improvement.
L102:   * Develop and implement a 【13†training evaluation plan】 that includes the evaluation purpose, questions, and data collection methods.
L103:   * Recruit evaluation participants who reflect your learner audience.
L104:   * Conduct a formative evaluation as part of development. This may include peer review, quality checklist assessment (e.g., using this checklist), pilot testing, or 【14†usability testing†www.usability.gov】.
L105:   * Conduct 【13†outcome evaluation】 that includes 【15†training effectiveness】 and learner assessment (Standard 7).
L106:   * Include opportunity for learners to provide feedback on training.
L107:     * Include open-ended feedback, if possible.
L108:   * Review and analyze evaluation data for training improvement.
L109:     * Plan to use 【13†process evaluation】 data and learner feedback for ongoing quality improvement.
L110:     * Make recommendations for training content, delivery methods, and learning activities that fill gaps with focus on areas with greatest need.
L111: Some trainings may require additional attributes. Consider if the following apply to your training:
L112: 
L113:   * Conduct a 【15†delayed or follow-up evaluation】 after learners have had time to apply what they learned.
L114: ## 7. Learner Assessment
L115: ### Training includes opportunity for learner assessment.
L116:   * Construct learner assessments (e.g., posttest, knowledge check, exercise, observed practice, question and answer session, or problem solving) that relate directly to learning objectives to reinforce learning.
L117:     * Use different question formats, such as multiple choice, matching, listing, reordering, and sorting.
L118:   * Use socially and contextually relevant assessments for learners to apply what they have learned (e.g., case scenarios are realistic and relevant to learners).
L119:   * Provide learners with feedback on their responses or skill demonstration to support learning.
L120: Some trainings may require additional attributes. Consider if the following apply to your training:
L121: 
L122:   * Recognize learner completion through a certificate or other notification.
L123: ## 8. Follow-up Support
L124: ### Training includes follow-up support for the learner.

L20: # Evaluate Training: Measuring Effectiveness
L21: 
L22: Oct. 28, 2024
L23: ## What to know
L24: 
L25:   * Effective trainings help learners gain knowledge and skills they can apply to their workplace.
L26:   * Determine the effectiveness of your training by understanding what to evaluate, when to evaluate, and what questions to ask learners.
L27: ## Overview
L28: 
L29: The goal of training is to help a learner improve their competence, capacity, and performance. Training helps learners gain new knowledge and skill. The most effective training also helps learners apply this information to their workplace, a process known as transfer of learning or simply learning transfer. Training effectiveness refers to how well your training supports learning and learning transfer. There are many ways to evaluate training effectiveness.
L30: ## What to evaluate
L31: 
L32: You should assess both learning and learning transfer, whenever possible.
L33: 
L34: ### Evaluate learning
L35: 
L36: Design your evaluation to assess how successfully the learner met the training's learning objectives. Look at the combined results for all learners to help you understand their learning and identify data trends that indicate challenging topics for your learners—which might show a need to improve course content or instruction.
L37: ### Evaluate learning transfer
L38: 
L39: Design your evaluation to assess how successfully the learner can apply what they learned when they return to the workplace. Look at the combined results for all learners to help you understand if learning transfer is occurring and which topics are challenging for learners to apply—which might show a need for follow-up support for the learners.
L40: ## When to evaluate training effectiveness
L41: 
L42: Your data collection methods and timing will depend on your evaluation questions. Determine what information you need while considering what is feasible. Your time, resources, and training scope should drive your evaluation approach.
L43: 
L44: ### Learn more
L45: 
L46: To learn more about training evaluation methods and questions see 【3†Evaluate Training: Building an Evaluation Plan】.
L47: ### Before and after training
L48: 
L49: The best way to evaluate any change in learning is through assessment before and after the training. Conduct a pretest before and a posttest after your training and then compare the results.
L50: 
L51: Considerations:
L52:   * The test can include a demonstration to assess skill in addition to knowledge, if needed.
L53:   * Using only a posttest, without a pretest, can provide an assessment of skill or knowledge proficiency. This allows you to know if learners achieved a certain level of knowledge or skill by the end of the training, but you will not know if there was a change in learning. Learners might have already had the knowledge or skill at the start of the training.
L54: ### Retrospective pre/post assessment
L55: 
L56: If you are unable to assess learning through a pretest and posttest, consider using a retrospective pre/post assessment that asks learners to self-assess their knowledge before and after the course as part of a postcourse evaluation.
L57: 
L58: ### Examples
L59: 
L60: 1. Rate your knowledge of the course topic before the course.
L61: 
L62: 2. Rate your knowledge of (or skill in) the course topic now after the course.
L63: ### During training
L64: 
L65: Build knowledge or skill assessment into the training, like knowledge checks, quizzes or observations. This can provide evaluation data and reinforce learning at the same time.
L66: 
L67: Considerations:
L68:   * In an e-learning, you might have knowledge checks throughout the course to help reinforce learning. Those same knowledge checks give you data on how learners progress during the course.
L69:   * For an in-person training, you might ask your learners questions to assess their comprehension or use an activity to gauge how they apply what they are learning. This provides real-time information for the instructor to reinforce content or adapt as needed.
L70: ### Immediately after training
L71: 
L72: In many situations, you might only be able to gather information from your learners immediately after the training ends. You can design your postcourse evaluation to assess learning and predict learning transfer immediately after the course ends, while learners are available to respond.
L73: 
L74: Considerations:
L75:   * Postcourse evaluations traditionally focus on learner satisfaction, but the research shows learner satisfaction does not determine a training's effectiveness.
L76:   * Postcourse evaluations cannot objectively assess learning or learning transfer, but focusing on the areas with the strongest, most consistent relationships with learning and learning transfer can provide you with meaningful data about training effectiveness.
L77:     * Based on 【4†factors that predict learning transfer】, Section 3 of the 【5†Recommended Training Effectiveness Questions for Postcourse Evaluations User Guide】 can help you determine your training's effectiveness.
L78: ### Delayed evaluation or follow-up
L79: 
L80: Delayed evaluation, also called follow-up evaluation, is the best way to assess learning transfer. This helps training developers understand how much information learners retained, and if they have applied what they learned on the job. You can follow-up with learners to assess learning transfer after they have had time to go back to their workplace and apply what they have learned.
L81: 
L82: Considerations:
L83:   * For some trainings, it might also be appropriate to follow-up with learners' supervisors.
L84:   * The timing of your delayed evaluation should be based on your program resources, the specific topic of the training, and learners' capacity to apply what they learned in the workplace.
L85: ## Recommended training effectiveness questions
L86: These questions focus on 【4†themes strongly associated with learning and learning transfer】 that can be measured in-person or online with adult learners. For more information, visit the 【5†Recommended Training Effectiveness Questions for Postcourse Evaluations User Guide】. The user guide includes the recommended questions, rationale for each question, additional context or caveats that you should consider when using the questions, and references to the research that supports the questions.
L87: You can adapt the questions to fit your training evaluation plan and data collection tools. The 【6†Example Postcourse and Follow-Up Evaluations】 use the Training Effectiveness questions along with additional questions that inform quality improvement and decision making.
